title: The secret of mirth (Chesterton, Orthodoxy 1908)
hook: Chesterton calls joy the gigantic secret of the Christian
tomorrow: if you could keep only five books for life, which would they be?

segments.voice: This week: a living flame, a pilgrim, a bishop's patience, a definite service, one step at a time, and a world charged with grandeur. Yesterday's line was charged with grandeur.
screen: `CHARGED WITH GRANDEUR.` → `THE WEEK, IN SIX LINES.`

segments.voice: Some people's feelings are all over their stories: tears at the movie, a rant about the ref. And then there's the one thing they keep to themselves. G. K. Chesterton, an English writer, ends his book Orthodoxy with a guess like that about Jesus. Tears, shown. Anger, shown. And one thing kept back. His guess isn't sorrow, and it isn't power.
screen: `TEARS, SHOWN. ANGER, SHOWN.` → `ONE THING KEPT BACK.`

segments.voice: Orthodoxy is the book in which Chesterton explains how he came to believe, and it saves its boldest idea for the last pages. First, the flip. He argues that people are more themselves when joy is the deep thing in them and grief the surface thing, not the other way round. Joy, he writes, "is the gigantic secret of the Christian." Second, what Jesus showed. Chesterton reads the Gospels and notices that Jesus didn't hide his tears; he wept openly, as when he saw his city from far off. He didn't hold back his anger either; he overturned the tables in the Temple. Third, what Jesus hid. Something, Chesterton says, he did keep back, something he hid when he went up a mountain alone to pray. Fourth, the guess, and it's the book's last sentence: "There was some one thing that was too great for God to show us when He walked upon our earth; and I have sometimes fancied that it was His mirth." Notice the words: sometimes fancied. He doesn't claim to know. After a whole book of arguing, he stops arguing, and ends with a guess, offered lightly, about laughter. If there's a joke in it, it's on nobody.
screen: `JOY DEEP, GRIEF ON THE SURFACE.` · `TEARS AND ANGER, SHOWN.` · `SOMETHING HIDDEN ON THE MOUNTAIN.` · `SOMETIMES FANCIED: HIS MIRTH.` · then, large: `THE GIGANTIC SECRET.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers three things that made you laugh this week, one for each breath, and let each one play again. If a laugh comes, let it out freely; if only a smile comes, that's enough. If you pray, you can offer the joy back as thanks.
The secret of mirth. Chesterton's closing guess: that what God kept hidden, walking on earth, was his joy. Today's word.
Your line: the gigantic secret. Six lines this week, and the last one laughs. That's the week.

fork.setup: at a wake, the cousins start telling their grandpa's funniest stories and the room laughs. an uncle frowns: not here. by Chesterton's last page, what's happening?
options: joy running underneath grief, where Chesterton thinks it belongs.
disrespect; grief should be the deepest thing in that room.
denial; laughing means they haven't accepted it yet.
fork.reveal: Chesterton argues people are most themselves when joy is fundamental and grief superficial, and guesses God's own hidden secret was mirth.
